To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) by using randomized simulated objects and a domain adaptation approach, we are able show that it is possible to train a deep learning based robotic grasping system to generalize to novel objects without collecting any real world data; and (2) by using unlabeled real world grasping images, we can train a grasping model that achieves real world grasping success rates similar to those achieved with 939K labeled real world samples.

(1) using simulated data and domain adaptation we can achieve real world performance that is similar to training on a large amount of real world data, and (2) using unlabeled real world images and our Grasp-GAN methodology we can achieve real-world performance that is similar that achieved using a large number of real world labels.

(1) by using simulated grasping data and domain adaptation we can reduce the number of physical test grasps needed to achieve a certain level of performance by 50 times, (2) by using only unlabled real data we can achieve real world grasping accuracy that is comparable to that achieved by 939,777 real world samples, and (3) we propose GraspGAN, a novel method for pixel level domain adaptation for grasping.
In summary, our research is concerned with
improving the efficiency of training robotic grasping systems using simulation and unlabeled real world samples.
the problem of how to train a robotic grasping system to generalize to new objects from raw RGB images.

the question of what are the minimal real world data requirements needed to train a deep learning based robotic grasping system, and how can we leverage synthetic data and domain transfer to achieve these goals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, using a combination of simulation and domain adaptation techniques, it is possible to achieve real world performance with orders of magnitude fewer real world samples than are typically needed.

we show that, by combining synthetic data and domain adaptive methods, we can significantly improve the efficiency of deep robotic grasping, and that we can achieve a similar level of performance to that achieved with large amounts of labeled real world data, by using only unlabled real world data.
, by combining synthetic data and domain adaption, we are able show that we can achieve similar performance as using only real world data, but with a much smaller amount of real world data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, by using simulation and domain adaptation, one can reduce the number of physical test grasps needed to achieve a certain level of performance, or, alternatively, achieve a similar level of performance with a much smaller number of physical test samples.

by using our approach we were able to achieve a 99.6% success rate on a novel object with 1000 unlabeled real world images and 10,000 simulated images, which is similar to the 99.9% success rate that we obtained with 10,000 unlabeled real world samples and 1000 labeled real world samples.

we are able to train an object independent grasping system that achieves 80% grasp success on novel objects in the real world, using 100 times less data compared to a system trained only on real world data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
by using a combination of simulation and domain adaptation, one can significantly improve the efficiency of training deep neural network grasping systems.
, even though simulators are not perfect, they can still be useful for learning robotic grasping models.
domain adaptation can significantly reduce the number of samples needed to learn a robust grasping system, and that this can be achieved with only a modest amount of real world unlabeled data.
